pl-l4d45c4-d1e115.summary: Raises the case of two men, rich and poor, equally and moderately good, who need suffrages and merited equally to be helped; for the rich man special and common prayers and many alms are given, for the poor only common prayers. Is the poor man helped as much by fewer aids as the rich by more? If not, he is not repaid by merit, having merited equally; if so, what did the special aids give the rich?

pl-l4d45c4-d1e118.summary: Answers that general and special aids together did not avail the rich more than general aids alone availed the poor; yet the special ones helped the rich not to something else or greater, but to the same, so that one benefit came from many causes.

pl-l4d45c4-d1e121.summary: Adds that it can also be said that the many aids gave the rich man a quicker, not a fuller, release.
claims: Additional suffrages may hasten, not increase, release.

pl-l4d45c4.summary: Asks about two equally, moderately good men, one rich and one poor, both needing suffrages: for the rich many special prayers and alms are made, for the poor only common prayers. If the poor is not helped equally, he is not repaid by merit; if he is, what did the special suffrages give the rich? Lombard answers that general and special suffrages did not avail the rich more than the general ones the poor, but helped him to the same end through more causes; or they gave him a quicker, not fuller, release.
claims: Equal merit receives equal benefit from suffrages.
Special suffrages may bring a quicker, not fuller, release.
